# Data wrangling with Tidier {#sec-tidier}

In the original book this is the `tidyverse` chapter. Julia has a remarkably faithful
translation: the [**Tidier**](https://tidierorg.github.io/Tidier.jl/stable/) family, a
pure-Julia reimplementation of the `tidyverse` mini-language on top of `DataFrames.jl`.

```{julia}
#| label: setup-05
using TidierData
using DataFrames
using Statistics
```

## The data {#sec-pond-data}

Throughout the book we use a **simulated** survey of anurans in 180 ponds across three
regions. The data are simulated on purpose: because the generating process is known,
every model fitted in @sec-linear-models and @sec-glm can be checked against the
truth. The generator lives in `scripts/make_data.jl`.

```{julia}
#| label: load-data
using CSV

ponds = CSV.read(joinpath("..", "data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame)
first(ponds, 5)
```

```{julia}
#| label: structure
describe(ponds, :eltype, :nmissing, :mean, :min, :max)
```

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pond_id` | pond identifier |
| `region` | region (Atlantic, Cerrado, Amazon) |
| `hydro` | hydroperiod (permanent, temporary) |
| `area_m2` | pond area (m²) |
| `canopy` | canopy cover (%) |
| `temp_c` | water temperature (°C) |
| `richness` | species richness (count) |
| `focal` | focal species occurrence (0/1) |
| `body_size` | mean body size (mm) |

```{julia}
#| label: checker-05
#| include: false
include(joinpath("..", "exercises", "check.jl"))
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}

## `@chain`: the pipe {#sec-chain}

`@chain` is the backbone of everything that follows. It passes each line's result as
the first argument of the next — exactly the role of `|>` (or `%>%`) in R.

```{julia}
#| label: chain-basic
@chain ponds begin
    @filter(region == "Amazon")
    @select(pond_id, area_m2, canopy, richness)
    @arrange(desc(richness))
    first(5)
end
```

::: {.r-equivalent}
**In R**

```r
ponds %>%
  filter(region == "Amazon") %>%
  select(pond_id, area_m2, canopy, richness) %>%
  arrange(desc(richness)) %>%
  head(5)
```

The correspondence is line for line. The only syntactic difference is the `@` and the
`begin ... end`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 5.1 — The largest ponds in the Cerrado

Write a `@chain` that returns the three largest ponds (by `area_m2`) in the Cerrado,
largest first. Store the result in `top3` and check it with `check("5.1", top3)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Three steps, one per line: keep the Cerrado rows, sort by area from largest to
smallest, keep the first three. The block above does something very similar.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-5-1
top3 = @chain ponds begin
    @filter(region == "Cerrado")
    @arrange(desc(area_m2))
    first(3)
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-5-1-check
check("5.1", top3)
```
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-5-1
#| include: false
Checks.verify("5.1", top3)
```

## The five verbs {#sec-verbs}

### `@filter` — pick rows

```{julia}
#| label: filter
@chain ponds begin
    @filter(richness > 8 && hydro == "permanent")
    nrow
end
```

Note: inside `@filter`, use `&&` and `||`, not `&` and `|` as in `dplyr`.

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 5.2 — Several conditions at once

How many temporary ponds have canopy cover above 60% **and** richness below the
overall median richness? Check the number with `check("5.2", n)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Compute the median first, outside the chain: `med = median(ponds.richness)`. Inside a
Tidier macro a bare name means a column, so to use the variable `med` write `!!med`.

If you get `TypeError: non-boolean (Missing) used in boolean context`, some ponds have
no canopy value, and `missing > 60` is neither true nor false. Remove those rows first
with `@drop_missing(canopy)` (@sec-tidier-missing).
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-5-2
med = median(ponds.richness)

n = @chain ponds begin
    @drop_missing(canopy)
    @filter(hydro == "temporary" && canopy > 60 && richness < !!med)
    nrow
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-5-2-check
check("5.2", n)
```

Dropping ponds without canopy is the right call here: we cannot know whether their
canopy is above 60%. The median, though, is computed on all 180 ponds, before
dropping anything.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-5-2
#| include: false
Checks.verify("5.2", n)
```

### `@select` — pick columns

```{julia}
#| label: select
@chain ponds begin
    @select(pond_id, region, richness)
    first(3)
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: select-negative
# exclusion and ranges work as in dplyr
@chain ponds begin
    @select(-pond_id, -focal)
    names
end
```

### `@mutate` — create columns

```{julia}
#| label: mutate
ponds_t = @chain ponds begin
    @mutate(
        log_area   = log(area_m2),
        canopy_std = (canopy - mean(skipmissing(canopy))) / std(skipmissing(canopy)),
        open       = canopy < 40,
    )
end

@chain ponds_t begin
    @select(pond_id, area_m2, log_area, canopy, canopy_std, open)
    first(5)
end
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 5.3 — Richness per 100 m²

Bigger ponds tend to hold more species. Add a column `rich_per_100m2` with the number
of species per 100 m² of pond, keeping every row and column of `ponds`. Store the
result in `ponds_d` and check it with `check("5.3", ponds_d)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`richness / area_m2` is species per m²; multiply by 100.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-5-3
ponds_d = @chain ponds begin
    @mutate(rich_per_100m2 = richness / area_m2 * 100)
end

check("5.3", ponds_d)
```
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-5-3
#| include: false
Checks.verify("5.3", ponds_d)
```

### `@group_by` + `@summarize` — aggregate

```{julia}
#| label: summarize
@chain ponds begin
    @group_by(region, hydro)
    @summarize(
        n            = n(),
        mean_rich    = mean(richness),
        sd_rich      = std(richness),
        prop_focal   = mean(focal),
    )
    @arrange(region, hydro)
end
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 5.4 — Where is the focal species?

Compute, for each region, the proportion of ponds where the focal species occurs, in a
column called `prop_focal`, sorted from highest to lowest. Check it with
`check("5.4", by_region)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`focal` is 0 or 1, so its mean is the proportion of ponds where it is 1. Sorting from
highest to lowest is `@arrange(desc(...))`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-5-4
by_region = @chain ponds begin
    @group_by(region)
    @summarize(prop_focal = mean(focal))
    @arrange(desc(prop_focal))
end

check("5.4", by_region)
```
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-5-4
#| include: false
Checks.verify("5.4", by_region)
```

### `@arrange` — sort

```{julia}
#| label: arrange
@chain ponds begin
    @arrange(region, desc(richness))
    @select(region, pond_id, richness)
    first(6)
end
```

## Missing data {#sec-tidier-missing}

The `canopy` column has missing values on purpose.

```{julia}
#| label: count-missing
sum(ismissing.(ponds.canopy))
```

```{julia}
#| label: drop-missing
@chain ponds begin
    @drop_missing(canopy)
    nrow
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: missing-summarize
# aggregating while ignoring missings
@chain ponds begin
    @group_by(region)
    @summarize(mean_canopy = mean(skipmissing(canopy)))
end
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`mean(canopy)` returns `missing` if any value is missing — the same behaviour as R's
`mean()` without `na.rm = TRUE`. Be explicit with `skipmissing`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 5.5 — Where are the gaps?

Before dropping missing values, it is worth knowing where they are: if they
concentrate in one region, dropping them changes that region more than the others.
Count, per region, how many ponds have no canopy value, in a column called
`n_missing`. Check it with `check("5.5", gaps)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`ismissing.(canopy)` gives `true` for each missing value, and `sum` counts the
`true`s. Both work inside `@summarize`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-5-5
gaps = @chain ponds begin
    @group_by(region)
    @summarize(n_missing = sum(ismissing.(canopy)))
end

check("5.5", gaps)
```

Seven missing values spread over three regions: no region is hit much harder than
the others, so dropping them is unlikely to bias comparisons between regions.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-5-5
#| include: false
Checks.verify("5.5", gaps)
```

## Long and wide formats {#sec-pivot}

```{julia}
#| label: pivot-longer
long = @chain ponds begin
    @select(pond_id, region, area_m2, canopy, temp_c)
    @pivot_longer(area_m2:temp_c, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")
end

first(long, 6)
```

```{julia}
#| label: pivot-wider
@chain long begin
    @pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = value)
    first(3)
end
```

## Joins {#sec-joins}

```{julia}
#| label: joins
# an auxiliary table with region-level information
regions = DataFrame(
    region     = ["Atlantic", "Cerrado", "Amazon"],
    biome_type = ["forest", "savanna", "forest"],
    mean_rain  = [1400, 1500, 2300],
)

@chain ponds begin
    @left_join(regions, region)
    @select(pond_id, region, biome_type, mean_rain, richness)
    first(5)
end
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 5.6 — Forest versus savanna

Using the `regions` table above, compute the mean richness of forest and savanna ponds,
in a column called `mean_rich`. Check it with `check("5.6", by_biome)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Join first, so every pond gets its `biome_type`; then group by `biome_type` and
summarize.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-5-6
by_biome = @chain ponds begin
    @left_join(regions, region)
    @group_by(biome_type)
    @summarize(mean_rich = mean(richness))
end

check("5.6", by_biome)
```
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-5-6
#| include: false
Checks.verify("5.6", by_biome)
```

## `DataFrames.jl` underneath {#sec-native-dataframes}

Tidier is a convenience layer. It is worth knowing the native form, which is what you
will meet in most of the ecosystem's documentation:

```{julia}
#| label: native-dataframes
combine(
    groupby(ponds, :region),
    :richness => mean => :mean_rich,
    :richness => length => :n,
)
```

Same result as the `@group_by`/`@summarize` above. Use Tidier to write, and recognize
the native form to read.

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 5.7 — The same, natively

Rewrite your answer to 5.4 with `groupby`, `combine` and `sort` from `DataFrames.jl`,
without Tidier macros. Check it with `check("5.7", by_region_native)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`sort(df, :col, rev = true)` sorts from highest to lowest.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-5-7
by_region_native = sort(
    combine(groupby(ponds, :region), :focal => mean => :prop_focal),
    :prop_focal, rev = true)

check("5.7", by_region_native)
```
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-5-7
#| include: false
Checks.verify("5.7", by_region_native)
```

## Challenges {.unnumbered}

These have no checker. They are about what the numbers do — and do not — tell you.

1. In 5.4 the Cerrado comes first, but the three proportions only range from 0.42 to
   0.48, each from 48 to 66 ponds. Open `scripts/make_data.jl`: does region affect the
   focal species in the simulation? What does that tell you about reading a ranking
   off a summary table?
2. In 5.6 forest ponds are richer than savanna ponds. But "forest" here means Atlantic
   plus Amazon. Compute mean richness per region and decide whether "forest" is a
   useful grouping for this question.
3. Use `@pivot_longer` to put `area_m2`, `canopy` and `temp_c` in one column, then
   compute the mean of each variable per region in a single pipeline. How do you deal
   with the missing canopy values?
